Data Quality Assessment, Missing Data Handling, Bias Detection, and Ethical Data Management in Sustainable Data Acquisition
Data Quality
Accuracy, completeness, consistency, validity, timeliness
Missing Data
Imputation, ML prediction, sensor fusion strategies
Bias Detection
Sensor, sampling, and algorithmic bias identification
Ethical Management
Privacy, transparency, minimization, lifecycle governance

Introduction
In sustainable data acquisition, the objective is not only to collect data using energy-efficient techniques such as adaptive sampling, duty cycling, wake-up radio, sensor scheduling, and in-sensor processing, but also to ensure that the collected data is accurate, complete, unbiased, and ethically managed. Poor-quality data can lead to incorrect analysis and unreliable decisions.
Energy-Efficient Collection
Adaptive sampling, duty cycling, wake-up radio, sensor scheduling, and in-sensor processing reduce acquisition overhead.
Data Integrity Requirements
Collected data must be accurate, complete, unbiased, and ethically managed to support reliable downstream decisions.
Consequence of Poor Quality
Poor-quality data leads to incorrect analysis and unreliable decisions — undermining the value of even the most efficient acquisition systems.

1. Data Quality Assessment
Data quality assessment is the process of evaluating whether the acquired sensor data is accurate, complete, consistent, valid, and timely before it is used for decision-making.
1
Accuracy
How close the sensor measurement is to the actual real-world value.
2
Completeness
Whether all required data values are available without missing records.
3
Consistency
Data from different sources follows the same format and rules.
4
Validity
Sensor data follows acceptable limits and defined value ranges.
5
Timeliness
Data is available when required for real-time or near-real-time decisions.

a) Accuracy
Definition
Accuracy determines how close the sensor measurement is to the actual real-world value.
Issues Affecting Accuracy
Sensor calibration errors
Hardware aging
Environmental interference
Sensor noise
Example: Smart Agriculture
A soil moisture sensor installed in a farm should measure actual soil moisture.
Actual Moisture
40%
Sensor Reading
65%
The inaccurate reading may cause the irrigation system to supply unnecessary water, leading to water wastage, increased energy consumption, and poor crop management.
Solution
Periodic sensor calibration
Comparing readings with reference sensors

b) Completeness
Definition: Completeness checks whether all required data values are available without missing records.
Example: Healthcare Monitoring System
A wearable heart-rate monitoring device records patient heartbeat every minute.
Expected data:
Time
Heart Rate
10:00
80 bpm
10:01
82 bpm
10:02
Missing

Missing readings may affect doctors' ability to detect abnormal conditions.
Redundant Sensors
Deploy backup sensors to capture readings when a primary sensor fails or is unavailable.
Data Recovery Mechanisms
Implement protocols that detect and recover lost transmissions before they create permanent gaps.
Predictive Filling of Missing Values
Use statistical or ML-based methods to estimate and fill missing data points based on surrounding patterns.

c) Consistency
Definition: Consistency ensures that data collected from different sources follows the same format and rules.
Example: Smart City Traffic Monitoring
Two sensors measure vehicle speed:
Sensor A
Speed = 60 km/hr
Sensor B
Speed = 16.6 m/sec
Both represent the same value but use different units. Without normalization, downstream analytics systems may treat these as different measurements, producing erroneous results.
Solution
Data normalization
Standard measurement formats
Why It Matters
Inconsistent units and formats across sensor networks are among the most common sources of silent data errors — errors that do not trigger alarms but corrupt analytical outputs.

d) Timeliness
Definition: Timeliness ensures that data is available when required.
Example: Smart Emergency Response System
Ambulance tracking sensors must provide real-time location data. Delayed GPS updates may result in:
Longer response time
Inefficient route planning
Solution
Real-time data transmission
Priority-based sensor scheduling
Key Principle
In time-critical applications, even accurate and complete data loses its value if it arrives too late to inform a decision.

e) Validity
Definition: Validity checks whether sensor data follows acceptable limits.
Example: Weather Monitoring System
Humidity values should normally be: 0% – 100%
Valid Range
0% – 100% relative humidity
Invalid Reading
Humidity = 150% — physically impossible; requires correction
If a sensor reports Humidity = 150%, the value is invalid and requires correction. Allowing invalid values to propagate into analytics pipelines can corrupt model outputs and trigger false alerts.
Range Checking
Automatically flag or reject readings that fall outside physically or operationally defined bounds.
Outlier Detection Algorithms
Statistical methods such as Z-score analysis or IQR filtering identify anomalous values for review or removal.

2. Missing Data Handling
Missing data occurs when sensor readings are unavailable due to battery saving modes, communication failures, sensor malfunction, or network problems. Handling missing data is important because incomplete datasets can reduce the accuracy of analytics models.
Battery Saving Modes
Duty cycling and sleep modes conserve energy but create intentional gaps in the data stream.
Communication Failures
Network outages, packet loss, or interference interrupt data transmission between sensor and server.
Sensor Malfunction
Hardware faults, physical damage, or firmware errors cause sensors to stop reporting values.
Network Problems
Congestion, routing failures, or protocol mismatches prevent data from reaching its destination.

a) Data Imputation
Missing values are estimated using existing data patterns.
Example: Temperature Monitoring
Time
Temperature
8 AM
28°C
9 AM
Missing → ≈29°C (interpolated)
10 AM
30°C
Using interpolation: 9 AM temperature ≈ 29°C. This avoids gaps in the dataset.

Using interpolation: 9 AM temperature ≈ 29°C. This avoids gaps in the dataset.
Linear Interpolation
Estimates missing values by drawing a straight line between the two nearest known data points — effective when data changes gradually and predictably.
Spline Interpolation
Uses smooth curves rather than straight lines, better capturing non-linear trends in sensor time series.
Forward/Backward Fill
Propagates the last known value forward (or the next known value backward) to fill short gaps — simple and computationally inexpensive.

b) Mean/Median Replacement
For small missing values, statistical methods can be used.
Example: Air Quality Sensor Readings
Known Values
45, 50, Missing, 55, 60
Calculation
(45 + 50 + 55 + 60) / 4 = 52.5
Result
Missing value replaced by approximately 52.5
Mean replacement is best suited for small, randomly distributed gaps. For larger or systematic gaps, more sophisticated methods such as ML-based prediction are preferred.

c) Machine Learning-Based Prediction
Advanced systems use ML models to estimate missing data.
Example: Smart Energy Meter
If electricity consumption data is missing for two hours, a prediction model can estimate usage based on:
Previous Consumption Pattern
Historical usage profiles reveal recurring daily and weekly cycles that inform accurate estimates.
Weather Conditions
Temperature and humidity data correlate strongly with energy demand, especially for heating and cooling loads.
Time of Day
Peak and off-peak usage patterns differ significantly, allowing time-aware models to produce more precise estimates.
This helps maintain continuous energy monitoring.

d) Sensor Fusion
Multiple sensors can compensate for missing information.
Example: Autonomous Vehicle
A self-driving car uses multiple sensing modalities simultaneously. If the camera fails due to poor visibility, LiDAR and radar provide supporting information.
Camera
Visual object recognition and lane detection
LiDAR
3D point cloud mapping; effective in low-light and fog
Radar
Velocity and distance measurement; robust in adverse weather

3. Bias Detection in Sensor Data
Bias detection identifies systematic errors or unfair patterns in collected data. Bias can affect the reliability and fairness of automated decisions.
Types of Bias
1
Sensor Bias
A sensor consistently produces incorrect measurements due to placement, exposure, or hardware degradation.
2
Sampling Bias
Collected data does not represent the complete environment because sensors are deployed non-uniformly.
3
Algorithmic Bias
AI models trained on biased data produce unfair or inaccurate results for underrepresented groups or regions.

a) Sensor Bias
Occurs when a sensor consistently produces incorrect measurements.
Example: Air Quality Monitoring
One pollution sensor is installed near a factory. Due to continuous exposure to smoke, it always shows higher pollution levels.
Result
Incorrect pollution estimation
Wrong environmental decisions
Solution
Sensor calibration
Multiple sensor deployment
Key Insight
Sensor bias is particularly dangerous because it is systematic — the sensor does not produce random errors but consistently skews in one direction, making the bias difficult to detect without a reference standard.

b) Sampling Bias
Occurs when collected data does not represent the complete environment.
Example: Smart City Traffic System
Traffic sensors are installed only on major highways. Data ignores small roads and residential areas.
What Is Captured
Major highway traffic volumes and speeds — well-instrumented and densely sampled.
What Is Missed
Small roads and residential areas — absent from the dataset entirely.
Result
Incorrect understanding of city-wide traffic patterns; biased routing recommendations.
Solution
Balanced sensor placement
Diverse data collection locations

c) Algorithmic Bias
Occurs when AI models trained on biased data produce unfair results.
Example: Healthcare Prediction System
A disease prediction model trained using data from only one region may perform poorly for patients from other regions. Differences in genetics, lifestyle, diet, and environmental exposure mean that a regionally trained model generalizes poorly to diverse populations.
Solution
Use diverse datasets
Evaluate model fairness
Broader Implication
Algorithmic bias is a downstream consequence of upstream data collection decisions. Addressing it requires intervention at both the data acquisition stage and the model evaluation stage.

Bias Detection Techniques
1
Statistical Analysis
Compare data patterns from different sources. Example: Comparing pollution readings from multiple city locations to identify abnormal sensors that consistently deviate from the group average.
2
Calibration and Validation
Regularly compare sensor readings with standard reference values. Example: Comparing smart meter readings with certified electricity meters to detect systematic offset or drift.
3
Fairness Evaluation
AI systems are tested to ensure equal performance across different groups. Example: A healthcare AI model should provide similar accuracy for different age groups, not just the demographic majority in the training data.

4. Ethical Data Management
Ethical data management ensures that collected data is handled responsibly while protecting privacy, security, and user rights.
1
Data Privacy
Sensitive information protected from unauthorized access through encryption and access control.
2
Data Transparency
Users informed about what data is collected, why, and who can access it.
3
Data Minimization
Only necessary data collected — reducing storage, energy, and privacy risk.
4
Responsible Sharing
Data shared without exposing sensitive or personally identifiable information.
5
Lifecycle Management
Data governed from collection through deletion across its complete operational life.

a) Data Privacy
Sensitive information should be protected from unauthorized access.
Example: Smart Healthcare System
Wearable devices collect highly sensitive personal health data including:
Heart rate
Sleep patterns
Physical activity
Protection Methods
Encryption
Access control
Data anonymization
Why It Matters
Health data is among the most sensitive categories of personal information. Unauthorized access can lead to discrimination, identity theft, or exploitation of vulnerable individuals.

b) Data Transparency
Users should know what data is collected, why it is collected, and who can access it.
Example: Smart Home System
A smart speaker should clearly inform users if it collects voice commands and user preferences.
What Data Is Collected
Users must be clearly informed of every data type captured — voice commands, usage patterns, location, preferences — with no hidden collection.
Why It Is Collected
The purpose of each data type must be disclosed — whether for service improvement, personalization, or third-party analytics.
Who Can Access It
Users must know which internal teams, partner organizations, or government bodies may access their data and under what conditions.

c) Data Minimization
Only necessary data should be collected.
Example: Smart Parking System
✔ Required Data
Parking slot availability — directly necessary for the system's core function.
✘ Not Required
Vehicle owner's personal information — unnecessary for slot availability and a privacy liability.
Benefits of Data Minimization
Less Storage
Smaller datasets reduce infrastructure costs and energy consumption.
Lower Energy
Transmitting and storing less data directly reduces the system's energy footprint.
Better Privacy
Data that is never collected cannot be breached, misused, or subpoenaed.

d) Responsible Data Sharing
Data should be shared without exposing sensitive information.
Example: Smart City Transportation
Traffic data can be shared for research after removing vehicle identity and aggregating location information.
Remove Vehicle Identity
Strip license plate numbers, registered owner details, and any unique vehicle identifiers before sharing datasets with researchers or third parties.
Aggregate Location Information
Replace precise GPS coordinates with zone-level or grid-level aggregates that preserve analytical utility while preventing individual tracking.
Share Anonymized Insights
The resulting dataset supports traffic research, urban planning, and policy decisions without compromising the privacy of individual road users.

e) Data Lifecycle Management
Data should be managed throughout its complete lifecycle:
Collection
Capture patient and sensor data securely
Storage
Encrypt and store data safely
Processing
Analyze and transform data for insights
Sharing
Control access for authorized users
Example: Healthcare Data
01
Collection
Sensors collect patient data at the point of care or through continuous wearable monitoring.
02
Storage
Data is encrypted during storage to prevent unauthorized access or data breaches.
03
Processing
Doctors access only authorized information relevant to their clinical role and patient relationship.
04
Deletion
Old unnecessary records are securely deleted to minimize exposure and comply with retention policies.

Integrated Case Study: Smart Agriculture Monitoring System
Scenario: A farm uses IoT sensors to monitor soil moisture, temperature, humidity, and crop health.
Sustainable Data Acquisition Methods
Adaptive Sampling
Sensor collects data frequently only when soil moisture changes significantly. During stable periods, sampling rate is reduced to conserve energy without sacrificing data fidelity.
Duty Cycling
Sensors remain inactive when conditions are stable. The system wakes sensors on a schedule or in response to threshold triggers, dramatically reducing power consumption.
Sensor Fusion
Combines soil, weather, and satellite data to produce a richer, more reliable picture of farm conditions than any single sensor type could provide alone.

Quality
Calibration, normalization, ML imputation, and outlier analysis ensure reliable sensor data throughout the farm network.
Bias

Ethics
